title: The Endless Lamp
subtitle: A Light That Never Runs Out

pages.text:
Come closer, my dear one, and look at this little clay lamp glowing in the dark. See how its small flame pushes away the shadows?

Tonight I want to tell you about a wise old teacher and a single tiny lamp that taught a whole roomful of children the most beautiful secret in the world.

Long ago, in a quiet forest school, a kind teacher gathered his students one evening. The hall was so dark they could barely see each other's faces.

In his hands the teacher held just one small lamp, its flame no bigger than a flower petal. Every child watched that one warm light.

The teacher said, 'Children, come and light your own lamps from mine.' But a thoughtful little boy frowned and held back.

'Teacher,' he whispered, 'if you give your light to all of us, won't your own flame grow smaller and smaller until it disappears?' It seemed a very sensible worry.

The teacher only smiled and gently touched his flame to the boy's lamp. With a soft little flicker, the boy's lamp burst into light.

'Now go,' said the teacher, 'and light the lamp of the child beside you.' So the boy did, and that child lit the next, and that one lit the next.

One lamp became two. Two became ten. Ten became a hundred. Soon the whole dark hall was glowing with warm golden light, and every single face was shining and happy.

The children laughed in wonder. From just one little flame, a whole ocean of light had been born.

Then the teacher lifted his own lamp high for everyone to see. 'Look carefully,' he said. 'Is my flame any smaller than before?'

The children gasped. His little flame was burning just as brightly as when the evening began. He had given his light to a hundred lamps, and lost nothing at all.

'This, my children, is how kindness works,' the teacher said softly. 'And love. And everything good you know. When you share them, you never have less — the whole world simply grows brighter.'

A kind word costs you nothing, yet it can light up someone's whole day. That is the magic of the endless lamp.

So tomorrow, my dear, share your light freely. Help a friend, teach what you know, give a smile to someone who is sad. You will lose nothing, and the world will glow a little more.

Now close your eyes and rest, my little lamp. Your light is safe and warm. Sleep well.

Settle in close, my dear one. Tonight's story is a little different — it is about a battlefield, but not the kind with swords and elephants.

It is about a secret battlefield that you visit every single day, even today. Can you guess where it is? Let me tell you.

Long ago there was a great, wide field called Kurukshetra, where the famous battle of the Mahabharata was fought.

But that field had another, more beautiful name. People also called it Dharmakshetra — which means 'the field of righteousness,' the field where you choose what is right.

Now why would a battlefield be called the field of doing right? Because the wise ones knew a deep truth.

The hardest battles in life are not fought with bows and arrows at all. They are fought quietly, inside our own hearts, where no one else can see.

Think about your own day, my dear. When you wanted to tell a little lie because the truth was scary — that was a tiny battle. When you wanted to keep the whole sweet but your heart said share it — that was a battle too.

When someone was unkind and you felt like being unkind back, but chose to stay gentle — that was the bravest battle of all.

Inside each of us, two little armies line up every day. On one side stand honesty, kindness, patience and courage.

On the other side stand the trickier feelings — anger, greed, jealousy and fear. They face each other on the field of your heart, just like the armies at Kurukshetra.

And here is the wonderful part: you are the one who decides which side wins. Not your friends, not your teacher — you.

Every time you choose the kind thing, the true thing, the patient thing, the good army grows a little stronger and braver inside you.

On that great field, Arjuna was not alone — wise Krishna stood beside him and guided him with calm, loving words.

You have a guide too. It is the quiet, good little voice inside you that always knows what is right. If you grow still and listen, you will hear it whispering.

So tomorrow, when you step onto your own field of righteousness, remember you are braver than any warrior. Choose the kind thing, even when it is the harder thing.

Now rest, my brave one. Today's battles are done, and you did well. Sleep peacefully.

Snuggle in, my dear one. Tonight I will tell you about a travelling theatre that came to a little town long ago, and the wisest actor who ever lived.

This is a gentle story that answers a very big question: who are you, really, deep down inside?

In the troupe was an actor so skilled that people came from far away just to watch him. He could become anyone at all.

One night he was a mighty king in golden robes. The next he was a poor beggar in rags. Then a fierce growling demon, then a giggling little child.

When he played the king, the whole crowd bowed and cheered. When he played the sad beggar, everyone wept real tears for him.

When he played the demon, the children hid behind their mothers! His acting was so real that people forgot it was only a play.

But each night, when the show ended and the curtain came down, something quiet and lovely happened.

The actor wiped away the paint, set down the golden crown or the beggar's bowl, and became simply himself again — calm, smiling, and the very same as always.

One evening a curious little boy crept up to him and asked, 'Weren't you so proud when you were the king? And weren't you terribly sad when you were the poor beggar?'

The actor laughed kindly and knelt down to answer. 'Ah,' he said, 'let me tell you my little secret.'

'All through the play,' he said, 'I never once forgot that the crown and the rags were only costumes. The king came and went. The beggar came and went.

But I, the one wearing them, stayed exactly the same underneath. So I could play every part happily, and never get lost in any of them.'

And here is the secret for you too, my dear. Each day you play many parts — a student, a friend, a big brother or sister. And feelings come and go like costumes: sometimes happy, sometimes cross, sometimes afraid.

But the real you, the calm and bright one wearing all those feelings, never changes. Moods are just costumes. They come, and they go.

So whatever costume tomorrow brings — a happy one or a difficult one — remember it is only for a little while. The peaceful you underneath is always there.

Now the curtain falls on today, my dear. Set down all your costumes and rest. Sleep well.

title: The Chariot of the Mind
subtitle: Holding the Reins of Your Senses

pages.text:
Come and lean on my shoulder, my dear one. Tonight I will show you a beautiful picture that the wise ones drew long, long ago to explain something tricky — your very own mind.

Close your eyes and imagine a grand chariot, pulled by five strong horses, racing across a wide plain.

The old sages said: a person is just like that chariot rolling through life. Every part of the chariot stands for a part of you.

Let me point them out one by one, and soon you will understand yourself in a whole new way.

Your body, they said, is the chariot itself — the thing that carries you about your day.

And your five senses — your eyes, ears, nose, tongue and skin — are five strong, eager horses. They always want to gallop off: toward sweets, toward shiny toys, toward every loud and exciting thing.

Now, what holds five wild horses together? The reins! And the reins, said the sages, are your mind.

Without reins, the horses bolt wherever they please — and the chariot bumps and crashes. That is what happens when our wishes pull us this way and that, with nothing to hold them.

But reins need clever hands to hold them. So who is the driver? The charioteer is your wisdom — the wise part of you that thinks, 'Is this a good idea? Should I stop, or go?'

A steady charioteer holds the reins firmly and gently, and guides the horses down the right road.

And riding inside the chariot, calm and still, sits the most important one of all — the true you, your own bright spirit.

The rider knows where it wants to go: to a beautiful place called peace, and goodness, and being your very best self.

Sometimes we let the horses run wild — one more sweet, one more hour of the screen, one big stormy temper. The reins slip, the charioteer dozes off, and the chariot goes crashing into the bushes.

We have all felt that crash, haven't we? The grumpy, tired, upside-down feeling when our horses ran away with us.

But a wise charioteer simply takes a slow, deep breath, picks up the reins again, and gently turns the horses home. That is all self-control really is — kindly holding your own reins.

Little by little, you become the calm driver of your own grand chariot, going wherever your good heart chooses.

Tonight, let your five horses rest in their stable. They have galloped all day and earned their sleep.

Tomorrow you will take up the reins again, calm and strong. Now rest, my little charioteer. Sleep well.

title: The Fish Who Saved the World
subtitle: The Story of Matsya and King Satyavrata

pages.text:
Listen, my dear one — can you hear the river in this story, softly flowing? Tonight I will tell you about a tiny, tiny fish, no bigger than your thumb, who once saved the whole wide world.

It begins with a good king and one small act of kindness.

Long ago there lived a gentle king named Satyavrata, who was kind to every living creature, great and small.

One morning, as he stood in the river offering water in his cupped hands, a tiny silver fish swam right into his palms and did something no fish had ever done — it spoke.

'Please, kind king,' the little fish begged, 'do not put me back in the river! The big fish will gobble me up. Won't you keep me safe?'

The king's heart melted at once. 'Do not be afraid, little one,' he said gently, and he carried the fish home in a small pot of water.

But by morning the fish had grown too big for the pot! So the king moved it to a large tub. By evening it had outgrown the tub, so he carried it to a pond.

Soon it was too big for the pond, and then too big for the river. At last the king gently set the enormous golden fish into the wide, deep ocean.

As the great fish slipped into the sea, it shone with a golden light, and the king understood that this was no ordinary fish. It was the Lord himself, come as Matsya to test the king's kind heart.

'You have cared for me with love,' said Matsya. 'Now I must warn you, dear king, of something very big that is coming.'

'In seven days,' said Matsya, 'a great flood will rise and cover the whole earth with water. But do not be afraid.'

'Build a mighty boat. Gather seeds of every plant, and a pair of every animal, and the wise ones too. When the waters come, I will return for you.'

The good king did exactly as he was told. And on the seventh day, dark clouds gathered and the rains poured down. The rivers swelled, the seas climbed higher, and water spread across all the land.

But the king and all his precious cargo floated safely upon the great boat, rocking on the endless waves.

Then, shining through the storm, the giant golden fish appeared once more. A great horn rose from its head, and the king tied the boat to it with a long, strong rope.

Gently, surely, Matsya pulled the little boat through the wild waters, all through the long dark days, keeping every life aboard safe and dry.

At last the rains stopped and the waters slowly sank away, leaving the green earth washed and new.

From the seeds and the animals and the wise ones the king had saved, life began again, fresh and beautiful. The whole world bloomed once more, all because one little fish had been shown kindness.

And so you see, my dear, no kind act is ever too small. The king saved a fish no bigger than your thumb, and that fish saved the entire world.

Whatever small kindness you do tomorrow may grow far greater than you can imagine. Now rest, my gentle one. Sleep well.
